claim: CD4+ T cells activated in the absence of methionine do not undergo normal cell growth/blastogenesis.
source: Flow cytometric forward and side scatter analysis of CD4+ T cells activated in the absence of methionine revealed that these cells do not undergo normal cell growth/blastogenesis (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing altered forward and side scatter profiles in Figure 1a.

claim: TCR-activated CD4+ T cells deprived of methionine are smaller than CD4+ T cells activated in the presence of methionine.
source: TCR-activated CD4+ T cells deprived of methionine are smaller than CD4+ T cells activated in the presence of methionine (Figure 1a)
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry scatter data in Figure 1a.

claim: CD4+ T cells activated without methionine fail to proliferate.
source: TCR-activated CD4+ T cells deprived of methionine are smaller than CD4+ T cells activated in the presence of methionine (Figure 1a), and fail to proliferate (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by cell count data over 48 hours shown in Figure 1b.

claim: CD69 activation marker is expressed normally in CD4+ T cells activated without methionine.
source: However activation markers such as CD69 are expressed normally (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1c showing CD69 expression.

claim: Serum methionine availability ranges from 3 to 30 μM.
source: Serum methionine availability has been shown to range from 3 to 30 μM (Mentch et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mentch et al., 2015.

claim: The frequency of IFNγ producing CD4+ T cells is dependent upon extracellular methionine availability.
source: The data in Figure 1d show that the frequency of IFNγ producing CD4+ T cells is dependent upon extracellular methionine availability (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1d showing IFNγ production at different methionine concentrations.

claim: A 2-fold reduction in methionine from 10 μM to 5 μM has a striking impact on the frequency of IFNγ producing CD4+ T cells under Th1 polarising conditions.
source: A 2-fold reduction in methionine from 10 μM to 5 μM thus had a striking impact on the frequency of IFNγ producing CD4+ T cells that could develop under Th1 polarising conditions (Figure 1e)
evidence: Supported by quantitative data in Figure 1e.

claim: Methionine availability controls the amount of IFNγ produced per CD4+ T cell.
source: A 2-fold reduction in methionine from 10 μM to 5 μM thus had a striking impact on the frequency of IFNγ producing CD4+ T cells that could develop under Th1 polarising conditions (Figure 1e) and also controlled the amount of IFNγ produced per cell (Figure 1f).
evidence: Supported by mean fluorescence intensity data in Figure 1f.

claim: Limiting extracellular methionine availability for 2 hr impacts the ability of activated T cells to maintain protein, RNA and DNA synthesis.
source: The data show that T cells activated in the presence of 100 μM methionine have high rates of protein, RNA and DNA synthesis (Figure 1g–i). However, limiting extracellular methionine availability for 2 hr strikingly impacted on the ability of the cells to maintain these key processes.
evidence: Supported by OPP, EU, and EdU incorporation data in Figures 1g-i.

claim: The EC50 for protein synthesis in TCR/CD28 activated CD4+ cells is 1.39 μM methionine.
source: The EC50, that is the concentration of methionine required for half maximal effect was in these TCR/CD28 activated CD4+ cells was 1.39 μM for protein synthesis
evidence: Calculated from dose-response curves shown in Figure 1j.

claim: The EC50 for RNA synthesis in TCR/CD28 activated CD4+ cells is 2.94 μM methionine.
source: The EC50, that is the concentration of methionine required for half maximal effect was in these TCR/CD28 activated CD4+ cells was 1.39 μM for protein synthesis; 2.94 μM for RNA synthesis
evidence: Calculated from dose-response curves shown in Figure 1k.

claim: The EC50 for the frequency of cells undergoing DNA synthesis in TCR/CD28 activated CD4+ cells is 12.62 μM methionine.
source: The EC50, that is the concentration of methionine required for half maximal effect was in these TCR/CD28 activated CD4+ cells was 1.39 μM for protein synthesis; 2.94 μM for RNA synthesis and 12.62 μM for the frequency of cells undergoing DNA synthesis (Figure 1j–l).
evidence: Calculated from dose-response curves shown in Figure 1l.

claim: The ability of Th1 cells to sustain RNA, protein and DNA synthesis is dependent on sustained methionine supply.
source: The data show that the ability of Th1 cells to sustain RNA, protein and DNA synthesis is also dependent on sustained methionine supply (Figure 1m–o).
evidence: Supported by data in Figures 1m-o showing reduced synthesis in methionine-limited conditions.

claim: Naïve CD4+ T cells have almost undetectable incorporation of extracellular 3H-methionine into protein.
source: Figure 2a shows naïve CD4+ T cells have almost undetectable incorporation of extracellular 3H-methionine into protein
evidence: Supported by radioactivity measurements in Figure 2a.

claim: Incorporation of 3H-methionine into protein is greatly increased upon TCR activation.
source: Figure 2a shows naïve CD4+ T cells have almost undetectable incorporation of extracellular 3H-methionine into protein, however incorporation of 3H-methionine into protein is greatly increased upon activation through the TCR (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by radioactivity measurements in Figure 2a showing time-dependent increase.

claim: TCR activated CD4+ T cells show an increase in the generation of S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) and homocysteine (HCy).
source: However, TCR activated cells show an increase in the generation of S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) and HCy (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by metabolomic analysis data in Figure 2b.

claim: Triggering the TCR drives increased flow through the methionine cycle.
source: This increased production of SAH and HCy demonstrates that triggering the TCR drives increased flow through the methionine cycle.
evidence: Inferred from increased SAH and HCy levels shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells accumulate 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and Methyl-5-thio-5-D-ribose 1-phosphate.
source: In this context, further evidence that TCR triggering drives the methionine cycle is provided by the data showing that activated CD4+ T cells accumulate 5-methylthioadenosine (MTA) and Methyl-5-thio-5-D-ribose 1-phosphate; metabolites produced downstream of polyamine synthesis.
evidence: Supported by metabolomic data in Figure 2b.

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells have increased levels of cystathionine and 2-oxobutanoate.
source: Activated CD4+ T cells also had increased levels of cystathionine and 2-oxobutanoate (C4H6O3); the latter is produced when cystathionine gamma-lyase converts cystathionine to cysteine (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by metabolomic data in Figure 2b.

claim: Trimethylation of both H3K4 and H3K27 in CD4+ T cells is increased upon in vitro TCR-stimulation.
source: These experiments show that trimethylation (me3) of both H3K4 and H3K27 in CD4+ T cells is increased upon in vitro TCR- stimulation (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2c.

claim: H3 trimethylation on K27 and K4 increases upon immune activation in vivo.
source: Analysis of the H3K27me3 and H3K4me3 staining shows that H3 trimethylation on K27 and K4 increases upon immune activation in vivo (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: Supported by in vivo adoptive transfer and immunization experiments shown in Figures 2e,f.

claim: The 3H-radiolabel from 3H-methionine is incorporated into RNA after 6 hr of TCR/CD28 stimulation.
source: The data show that the 3H-radiolabel is incorporated into RNA after 6 hr of TCR/CD28 stimulation, and this is further increased after 18 hr (Figure 2g).
evidence: Supported by radioactivity measurements in purified RNA shown in Figure 2g.

claim: SAH levels in TCR activated CD4+ T cells and Th1 cells are dependent upon extracellular methionine supply.
source: Figure 2i shows that SAH levels in TCR activated CD4+ T cells and Th1 cells are dependent upon extracellular methionine supply which argues that sustained methionine availability is required to produce methyl donors for protein and nucleotide methylation (Figure 2i).
evidence: Supported by ELISA measurements in Figure 2i.

claim: The increase in H3K4 and H3K27 trimethylation in CD4+ T cells in response to TCR activation is regulated by extracellular methionine availability.
source: In this context, the data in Figure 2j show that the increase in H3K4 and H3K27 trimethylation in CD4+ T cells in response to TCR activation is regulated by extracellular methionine availability (Figure 2j).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 2j.

claim: The percentage of total m6A methylation in effector Th1 cells decreases as extracellular methionine is decreased.
source: The data in Figure 2k show that the percentage of total m6A methylation in effector Th1 cells decreases as extracellular methionine is decreased (Figure 2k).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 2k.

claim: The amount of m5C in mRNA from effector Th1 cells is dependent upon extracellular methionine.
source: The data in Figure 2l show that the amount of m5C in mRNA from effector Th1 cells is dependent upon extracellular methionine (Figure 2l).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 2l.

claim: Naïve CD4+ T cells express the key methionine cycle enzymes MAT2A, AHCY and MTR.
source: The data show that naïve CD4+ T cells express the key methionine cycle enzymes MAT2A, AHCY and MTR (Figure 3c,d and e).
evidence: Supported by quantitative proteomics data in Figures 3c-e.

claim: Both MAT2A and AHCY are highly abundant proteins in the naïve cell proteomic landscape.
source: Interestingly, both MAT2A and AHCY are highly abundant proteins in the naïve cell proteomic landscape (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: Supported by protein copy number data in Figures 3c and 3d.

claim: SRM/SMS and MTAP are abundantly expressed in naïve T cells.
source: Similarly, SRM/SMS and MTAP, enzymes which use SAM for polyamine synthesis and subsequent methionine salvage, are abundantly expressed in naïve T cells (Figure 3f and g).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figures 3f and 3g.

claim: mtnA-D enzymes are expressed at levels higher than the 'average' protein in a T cell.
source: mtnA-D, enzymes involved in the final steps of methionine salvage, are also expressed at levels higher than the 'average' protein is expressed in a T cell (Figure 3h).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figure 3h.

claim: The relative abundance of methionine cycle enzymes is consistently maintained at high levels upon activation and differentiation of CD4+ T cells.
source: The relative abundance, as indicated by their concentration, of these proteins within the total proteomic landscape is consistently maintained at high levels upon activation and differentiation of CD4+ T cells (Figure 3i).
evidence: Supported by comparative proteomics data in Figure 3i.

claim: RNMT and CMTR1 are abundantly expressed in naïve and at similar levels in TCR activated CD4+ T cells.
source: The proteomics data show that RNMT and CMTR1 are abundantly expressed in naïve and at similar levels in TCR activated CD4+ T cells, whereas CMTR2 is not expressed at high levels in any population (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figure 4a.

claim: CMTR2 is not expressed at high levels in any CD4+ T cell population.
source: The proteomics data show that RNMT and CMTR1 are abundantly expressed in naïve and at similar levels in TCR activated CD4+ T cells, whereas CMTR2 is not expressed at high levels in any population (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figure 4a.

claim: Naïve T cells express equimolar levels of the METTL3/METTL14 m6A methyltransferase complex.
source: The data show that naïve T cells also express equimolar levels of the METTL3/METTL14 m6A methyltransferase complex (Figure 4b) (Liu et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figure 4b and citation to Liu et al., 2014b.

claim: Naïve T cells express high levels of NSUN2, and these high levels are maintained after TCR activation and through differentiation.
source: The proteomics data show that naïve T cells express high levels of NSUN2, the methyltransferase responsible for RNA m5C modification, these high levels are maintained after TCR activation and through differentiation (Figure 4c) (Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figure 4c and citation to Yang et al., 2017.

claim: The expression of the DNA methyl transferases DNMT1 and DNMT3a is markedly higher in immune activated CD4+ T cells than in naïve T cells.
source: The expression of the DNA methyl transferases DNMT1 and DNMT3a is markedly higher in immune activated CD4+ T cells than in naïve T cells (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figure 4d.

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells dramatically increase expression of UHRF1.
source: Moreover, activated CD4+ T cells dramatically increase expression of UHRF1, which is required for DNMT1 recruitment and activity (Nishiyama et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figure 4d and citation to Nishiyama et al., 2016.

claim: The expression of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) is highly increased upon T cell activation and in differentiated effector T cells compared with naïve T cells.
source: The expression of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which is responsible for histone 3 lysine 27 methylation (H3K27), is also highly increased upon T cell activation and in differentiated effector T cells compared with naïve T cells (Figure 4e,f)
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figures 4e and 4f.

claim: The protein expression profile of Th1 CD4+ T cells did not significantly vary upon acute methionine deprivation, with a correlation coefficient of 0.98.
source: The data shows that the protein expression profile did not significantly vary upon acute methionine deprivation, with a very high correlation coefficient between the two conditions of 0.98 (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by proteomics correlation analysis in Figure 5a.

claim: Acute short term methionine deprivation of Th1 cells had no impact on expression of key methionine cycle enzymes including MAT2A, AHCY, SRM/SMS, MTAP and mtnA.
source: With regard to the methionine cycle specifically, these experiments found that acute short term methionine deprivation of Th1 cells had no impact on expression of key enzymes including; MAT2A, AHCY, SRM/SMS,MTAP and mtnA (Figure 5c–g).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figures 5c-g.

claim: The expression of RNA, DNA and histone methyl transferases was not changed by short-term methionine restriction.
source: The expression of RNA, DNA and histone methyl transferases was also not changed by short-term methionine restriction (Figure 5h–j).
evidence: Supported by proteomics data in Figures 5h-j.

claim: The induction of GFP-Myc expression in response to TCR/CD28 activation is blunted in the absence of methionine.
source: The data show that the induction of GFP-Myc expression in response to TCR/CD28 activation is blunted in the absence of methionine (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 6a and 6b.

claim: mTORC1 activity in T cells is partially sensitive to methionine deprivation.
source: The data show mTORC1 activity in T cells was partially sensitive to methionine deprivation, though the impact of methionine loss was not equivalent to total amino acid deprivation or rapamycin treatment (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: Supported by phospho-S6 staining data in Figures 6c and 6d.

claim: Treatment with SAM modestly restores mTORC1 activity in the absence of methionine.
source: Treatment with SAM (50μM) modestly restores mTORC1 activity in the absence of methionine (Figure 6e,f).
evidence: Supported by phospho-S6 staining data in Figures 6e and 6f.

claim: Naïve CD4+ T cells show very little/near undetectable uptake of 3H-labeled methionine.
source: Naïve CD4+ T cells show very little/near undetectable uptake of 3H-labeled methionine (Figure 7a)
evidence: Supported by radiotracer uptake measurements in Figure 7a.

claim: Methionine transport is readily detected in CD4+ T cells activated with CD3/CD28 crosslinking antibodies and in effector Th1 cells.
source: Naïve CD4+ T cells show very little/near undetectable uptake of 3H-labeled methionine (Figure 7a) whereas methionine transport was readily detected in CD4+ T cells activated with CD3/CD28 crosslinking antibodies and in effector Th1 cells (Figure 7a).
evidence: Supported by radiotracer uptake measurements in Figure 7a.

claim: The high levels of methionine transport in Th1 cells is dependent on sustained signalling via the IL2 receptor.
source: Figure 7b show that the high levels of methionine transport in Th1 cells is dependent on sustained signalling via the IL2 receptor.
evidence: Supported by methionine uptake data at different IL2 concentrations in Figure 7b.

claim: 3H-methionine uptake in CD4+ effector Th1 cells is blocked by BCH.
source: The data show that 3H-methionine uptake in CD4+ effector Th1 cells is blocked by BCH.
evidence: Supported by uptake inhibition data in Figure 7d.

claim: Competition by Alanine, Lysine or MeAIB has little impact on methionine transport in activated CD4+ T cells.
source: The data also show that competition by either Alanine, Lysine or MeAIB which would block System A mediated uptake has little impact on methionine transport in activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by competitive uptake data in Figure 7d.

claim: 3H-methionine uptake in effector CD4+ T cells is sodium independent.
source: Furthermore, 3H-methionine uptake in effector CD4+ T cells is sodium independent (Figure 7e).
evidence: Supported by uptake data in sodium-free buffer in Figure 7e.

claim: Glutamine uptake in effector CD4+ T cells is not affected by BCH and is sodium dependent.
source: This contrasts with glutamine uptake in the same effector cells, which is not affected by BCH and is sodium dependent (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: Supported by glutamine uptake data in Figures 7e and 7f.

claim: Methionine transport in activated T cells is via System L transporters.
source: Collectively these data establish that methionine transport in activated T cells is via System L transporters.
evidence: Inferred from pharmacological characterization data in Figures 7d-f.

claim: The cellular uptake of the System L substrate 3H-phenylalanine is competitively inhibited by methionine.
source: Further evidence for this conclusion is shown in Figure 6g: the cellular uptake of the System L substrate 3H-phenylalanine is competitively inhibited by methionine (Figure 7h)
evidence: Supported by competitive uptake data in Figure 7g (text refers to 7h but figure is 7g).

claim: 3H-methionine incorporation into protein in activated T cells is blocked by the System L transport inhibitor BCH.
source: 3H-methionine incorporation into protein in activated T cells is blocked by the System L transport inhibitor BCH (Figure 7h)
evidence: Supported by protein incorporation data in Figure 7h.

claim: TCR induced production of methylated RNA is prevented in the presence of BCH.
source: TCR induced production of methylated RNA is prevented in the presence of BCH (Figure 7i)
evidence: Supported by RNA methylation data in Figure 7i.

claim: BCH treatment reduces SAH levels in TCR activated CD4+ T cells.
source: BCH treatment reduces SAH levels in TCR activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 7j)
evidence: Supported by SAH ELISA data in Figure 7j.

claim: m6A mRNA methylation is reduced in the presence of BCH.
source: m6A mRNA methylation is reduced in the presence of BCH (Figure 7k).
evidence: Supported by m6A ELISA data in Figure 7k.

claim: SLC7A5 null CD4+ T cells do not increase methionine uptake in response to activation with CD3/CD28 antibodies.
source: Figure 7l shows that SLC7A5 null CD4+ T cells do not increase methionine uptake in response to activation with CD3/CD28 antibodies.
evidence: Supported by methionine uptake data in SLC7A5 knockout cells in Figure 7l.

claim: SLC7A5 null CD4+ T cells show a striking decrease in their ability to increase levels of the methionine metabolite SAH in response to TCR/CD28 stimulation.
source: SLC7A5 null CD4+ T cells T cells also show a striking decrease in their ability to increase levels of the methionine metabolite SAH in response to TCR/CD28 stimulation (Figure 7m).
evidence: Supported by SAH measurements in SLC7A5 knockout cells in Figure 7m.

claim: Antigen receptor triggering of T cells initiates a cycle of methionine metabolism that generates the methyl donors required for RNA and histone methylation.
source: The present study explores how T cells control a fundamental metabolic pathway and shows that antigen receptor triggering of T cells initiates a cycle of methionine metabolism that generates the methyl donors required for RNA and histone methylation.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript including metabolomics, methylation assays, and uptake studies.

claim: A critical, rate limiting step to fuel protein synthesis and the methionine cycle in T cells is antigen receptor and cytokine regulation of methionine transport across the cell membrane.
source: We establish that a critical, rate limiting step to fuel protein synthesis and the methionine cycle in T cells is antigen receptor and cytokine regulation of methionine transport across the cell membrane.
evidence: Supported by data showing that methionine transport is upregulated upon TCR activation and IL2 signaling, and that transport inhibition blocks downstream processes.

claim: Naïve T lymphocytes express high levels of all the key methionine cycle enzymes but cannot transport sufficient methionine to provide the substrates for these enzymes or to fuel protein synthesis.
source: Naïve T lymphocytes express high levels of all the key methionine cycle enzymes but cannot transport sufficient methionine to provide the substrates for these enzymes or to fuel protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by proteomics data showing enzyme expression in naïve cells and uptake data showing minimal methionine transport.

claim: The sodium independent System L amino acid transporter, SLC7A5 is the dominant methionine transporter in activated T cells.
source: Previous studies have shown that SLC7A5 is important for T cell differentiation in vitro and in vivo (Sinclair et al., 2013) and proposed that this reflected the role of SLC7A5 as the key leucine transporter in activated T cells and its subsequent role in regulating the activity of the leucine sensing kinase mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1). The present data provide additional novel information as to why SLC7A5 is critically important for T cells; it is required to transport methionine.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological characterization, proteomics, and genetic knockout data showing SLC7A5 is necessary for methionine transport.

claim: T cells cannot rely on methionine salvage pathways or autophagy of intracellular cargo to meet their demands for methionine.
source: The dependence of T cell activation, differentiation and proliferation on extracellular methionine was striking and indicates that T cells cannot rely on methionine salvage pathways or autophagy of intracellular cargo to meet their demands for methionine.
evidence: Inferred from the strong dependence on extracellular methionine despite expression of salvage pathway enzymes.

claim: The most critical rate limiting step for mRNA translation is the rate of methionine transport via the System L transporter SLC7A5.
source: The present data highlight that the most critical rate limiting step for mRNA translation is the rate of methionine transport via the System L transporter SLC7A5 because it is this transporter that determines intracellular methionine bioavailability.
evidence: Inferred from data showing that methionine transport is rate-limiting and SLC7A5 is the dominant transporter.

claim: Methionine availability and SAM production modulate mTORC1 activity in T cells.
source: Methionine availability and SAM production also modulate mTORC1 activity in T cells analogous to the recently described methionine/SAM sensing pathways that regulate mTORC1 in HEK 293 T cells (Gu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by data showing partial sensitivity of mTORC1 to methionine deprivation and restoration with SAM, and citation to Gu et al., 2017.

claim: Engagement of the TCR induces RNA methylation.
source: The data herein give new insights namely that engagement of the TCR induces RNA methylation and it is the ability of TCR triggering to control methionine transport to fuel the methionine cycle that allows the TCR to control RNA methylation.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased RNA methylation upon TCR activation and dependence on methionine transport.

claim: The TCR does not control expression of the RNA methyltransferases; these are already present in naive T cells.
source: In this context the TCR does not control expression of the RNA methyltransferases; these are already present in naive T cells.
evidence: Supported by proteomics data showing similar expression of RNA methyltransferases in naïve and activated cells.

claim: Immune activated T cells dramatically upregulate lipid production programs to meet the demand for membrane biosynthesis associated with growth and proliferation.
source: Activated T cells also dramatically upregulate lipid production programs to meet the demand for membrane biosynthesis associated with growth and proliferation (Kidani et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kidani et al., 2013.

claim: T cells need a supply of glucose, leucine and arginine to sustain the activity of mTORC1.
source: T cells also need a supply of glucose, leucine and arginine to sustain the activity of the serine/threonine kinase complex Mammalian Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1) (Finlay et al., 2012; Nicklin et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Finlay et al., 2012; Nicklin et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015.

claim: mTORC1 is a critical kinase that regulates the differentiation and migratory capacity of effector T cells.
source: T cells also need a supply of glucose, leucine and arginine to sustain the activity of the serine/threonine kinase complex Mammalian Target of Rapamycin Complex 1 (mTORC1) (Finlay et al., 2012; Nicklin et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2015), a critical kinase that regulates the differentiation and migratory capacity of effector T cells (Delgoffe et al., 2011; Sinclair et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Delgoffe et al., 2011; Sinclair et al., 2008.

claim: Serine is required for biosynthesis of purine nucleotides needed for T cell proliferation.
source: serine is required for biosynthesis of purine nucleotides needed for T cell proliferation (Ma et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2017.

claim: Histone and DNA methylations are key epigenetic modifications that control the accessibility of DNA to the transcriptional machinery.
source: Histone and DNA methylations are key epigenetic modifications that control the accessibility of DNA to the transcriptional machinery (Allis and Jenuwein, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Allis and Jenuwein, 2016.

claim: mRNA cap methylation controls mRNA binding to the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) to regulate translation initiation.
source: mRNA cap methylation controls mRNA binding to the eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4E (eIF4E) to regulate translation initiation (Aregger and Cowling, 2017; Gonatopoulos-Pournatzis and Cowling, 2014; Varshney et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Aregger and Cowling, 2017; Gonatopoulos-Pournatzis and Cowling, 2014; Varshney et al., 2018.

claim: The methylation of adenosine, 'm6A', in RNA controls multiple processes including translation, splicing and stability of mRNA.
source: the methylation of adenosine, 'm6A', in RNA controls multiple processes including translation, splicing and stability of mRNA (Dominissini et al., 2012; Louloupi et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Mauer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dominissini et al., 2012; Louloupi et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017; Mauer et al., 2017.

claim: Protein arginine methylation is critical for T lymphocyte activation.
source: Furthermore, there is an increasing awareness that protein arginine methylation is critical for T lymphocyte activation (Inoue et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inoue et al., 2018.

claim: Methionine is an essential amino acid in mammals for de novo protein synthesis.
source: In this context, methionine is an essential amino acid in mammals for de novo protein synthesis but it is also required for the production of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor for DNA, RNA and protein methyltransferases.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Methionine is required for the production of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor for DNA, RNA and protein methyltransferases.
source: In this context, methionine is an essential amino acid in mammals for de novo protein synthesis but it is also required for the production of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor for DNA, RNA and protein methyltransferases.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: SAM levels remain relatively constant between TCR stimulated and naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: The T cell metabolomics data show that SAM levels remain relatively constant between TCR stimulated and naïve CD4+ T cells (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by metabolomics data in Figure 2b.

claim: Methionine synthase (MTR) and the cofactor vitamin B12 perform the rate-limiting step of incorporating methyl groups derived from folate metabolism and HCy to produce methionine in the de novo pathway.
source: In the de novo pathway, methionine synthase (MTR) and the cofactor vitamin B12 perform the rate-limiting step of incorporating methyl groups derived from folate metabolism and HCy to produce methionine.
evidence: This describes established biochemical pathway knowledge.

claim: The sulphur of MTA can be recycled back into methionine using the salvage pathway, the first step of which is catalysed by MTA phosphorylase (MTAP).
source: The sulphur of MTA can be recycled back into methionine using the salvage pathway, the first step of which is catalysed by MTA phosphorylase (MTAP) to generate 5-methylthioribose-1-phosphate (reviewed in Mentch and Locasale, 2016; Albers, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to review articles Mentch and Locasale, 2016; Albers, 2009.

claim: In vivo activated CD8+ T cells exhibit dynamic control of translation as they differentiate from naïve (low translation rates) into effector (high translation rates) and memory (low translation rates) cells.
source: In this latter context, it has been shown that in vivo activated CD8+ T cells exhibit dynamic control of translation as they differentiate from naïve (low translation rates) into effector (high translation rates) and memory (low translation rates) cells (Araki et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Araki et al., 2017.

claim: SLC7A5 expression is restricted to TCR activated effector cells and low in naïve and memory T cells.
source: We have previously shown that SLC7A5 expression is restricted to TCR activated effector cells and low in naïve and memory T cells (Sinclair et al., 2013; Preston et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sinclair et al., 2013; Preston et al., 2015.

claim: Dietary methionine restriction has been shown to alter histone methylation in the liver.
source: Extracellular methionine availability in plasma is thus dependent upon dietary intake and dietary methionine restriction has been shown to alter histone methylation in the liver (Mentch and Locasale, 2016; Mentch et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mentch and Locasale, 2016; Mentch et al., 2015.

claim: RPMI tissue culture media contains 100 μM methionine.
source: Methionine levels in RPMI tissue culture media are 100 μM.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the composition of standard tissue culture media.

claim: Immune activated T lymphocytes modulate the activity of key metabolic pathways to support transcriptional reprograming and reshaping of cell proteomes that permits effector T cell differentiation.
source: Immune activated T lymphocytes modulate the activity of key metabolic pathways to support the transcriptional reprograming and reshaping of cell proteomes that permits effector T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general principle supported by the study.

claim: Only T cells that respond to antigen to upregulate and sustain methionine transport are supplied with methyl donors that permit the dynamic nucleotide methylations and epigenetic reprogramming that drives T cell differentiation.
source: Only T cells that respond to antigen to upregulate and sustain methionine transport are supplied with methyl donors that permit the dynamic nucleotide methylations and epigenetic reprogramming that drives T cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: The regulation of methionine transport licenses use of methionine for multiple fundamental processes that drive T lymphocyte proliferation and differentiation.
source: These data highlight how the regulation of methionine transport licenses use of methionine for multiple fundamental processes that drive T lymphocyte proliferation and differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the study's findings.

claim: Activated T cells accelerate glucose metabolism to fuel oxidative phosphorylation, glycolysis and the production of UDP-GlcNAc to allow critical intracellular protein O-GlcNAcylations.
source: For example, activated T cells accelerate glucose metabolism to fuel oxidative phosphorylation, glycolysis and the production of UDP-GlcNAc to allow critical intracellular protein O-GlcNAcylations (Donnelly and Finlay, 2015; Swamy et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donnelly and Finlay, 2015; Swamy et al., 2016.

claim: T lymphocytes responding to antigen undergo rapid proliferation as they differentiate to produce effector populations.
source: T lymphocytes responding to antigen undergo rapid proliferation as they differentiate to produce effector populations.
